subjects.displayTitle: Reason: learning to examine what we believe
subjects.introduction: Inherited opinion is a comfortable place to live, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá keeps asking people to leave it: test what you hear against reason and science, He says, and treat a conception without decisive proof as a wave on the ocean of imagination, here one hour and gone the next. He defines reason plainly as the movement from known premises to a conclusion not yet known, and He turns it against the philosophers who would accept nothing they could not sense, reminding them that the eye sees the shore move when the ship does, and that a cow senses nothing beyond the animal world without being the greatest of philosophers. Aristotle’s account of what a demonstration requires, true premises standing in the right explanatory order, is a bracing companion [1]. Yet proofs are a road, not a destination: once the heart turns toward the Sun of Truth, it recognizes the Sun by its own light. From here the journey runs to the independent investigation of truth, to the limits of the intellect, and to the proofs for the existence of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with active examination, distinguish inference from sensation, test the limits of arguments, and end with learning directed toward recognition and service.

order.why: Open with the invitation to examine rather than inherit conclusions.
shortened: The intellectual proofs of Divinity are based upon observation and evidence which constitute decisive argument, logically proving the reality of Divinity, the effulgence of mercy, the certainty of inspiration and immortality of the spirit. This is, in reality, the science of Divinity.

In divine questions we must not depend entirely upon the heritage of tradition and former human experience; nay, rather, we must exercise reason, analyze and logically examine the facts presented so that confidence will be inspired and faith attained. Then and then only the reality of things will be revealed to us.

order.why: Distinguish evidence from passing waves of thought.
Read the stated relation of claims to science and reason.
shortened: Whatever one hears must be tested against divine reason and science - if science and reason accept it, it is truth. But if universal science and true reason do not confirm it in any way, it is ignorance.

order.why: Give reasoning a concise account in terms of premises and conclusions.
Question the restriction of knowledge to sensation.
Examine examples of the senses misleading an observer.
shortened: I said human beings' best sense is eyesight, and it errs and sees wrongly. For instance, when a ship is moving, the eye sees the shores moving. I asked, "Do you consider the earth stationary and the planets moving, or vice versa?" They said, "Vice versa." I said, "The eye sees the earth as stationary and the planets as moving."

order.why: Distinguish failure to sense from proof of nonexistence.
Study a historical example of inference from signs.
Bring the rational mind to the inquiry into mysteries.
Encourage sustained study of proofs and evidence.
Include both spoken and written forms of argument.
Consider the kind of book that could aid inquiry.
shortened: In this day, the most useful books are those which demonstrate the validity of the Cause with logical proofs, intellectual evidences and spiritual arguments.

order.why: Ask how unreasonable inherited practices can obscure religion.
Explore arguments as a guide toward recognition. Return to the sun recognized through its own light.
Distinguish external proofs from inner experience.
shortened: These are theoretical arguments adduced for weak souls, but if the eye of inner vision be opened, a hundred thousand clear proofs will be seen. Thus, when man feels the indwelling spirit, he is in no need of arguments for its existence; but for those who are deprived of the grace of the spirit, it is necessary to set forth external arguments.

order.why: Presents a specific rational argument for immortality from the soul’s freedom from material composition.
Read the reported contrast between reasoning step by step and direct sight.
Consider the purpose assigned to the fruits of learning.
Turn rational inquiry toward religious unity and peace.
Close the linked readings with the social purpose of intellect.
Retain the historical illustration of disagreement among reasoners.
shortened: They would even change their own views: for twenty years they would deduce the existence of something through rational arguments, and then afterwards they would disprove the same, again through rational arguments. Even Plato at first proved through rational arguments the immobility of the earth and the movement of the sun, and then subsequently established, again through rational arguments, the centrality of the sun and the movement of the earth. Then the Ptolemaic theory became widespread and Plato's theory was entirely forgotten until a modern astronomer revived it. Thus have the mathematicians disagreed among themselves, even though they all relied on rational arguments.

order.why: Read understanding and the senses as related gifts.
shortened: First and foremost among these favors, which the Almighty hath conferred upon man, is the gift of understanding. His purpose in conferring such a gift is none other except to enable His creature to know and recognize the one true God—exalted be His glory. This gift giveth man the power to discern the truth in all things, leadeth him to that which is right, and helpeth him to discover the secrets of creation. Next in rank, is the power of vision, the chief instrument whereby his understanding can function.

order.why: Return to the importance of learning clear arguments.
shortened: Today there is no matter more important than studying and teaching clear proofs and conclusive divine evidence, for it is the source of life and path of salvation. In all regions of the world there are souls who are eagerly waiting to hear divine proofs and arguments, but due to the scarcity of teachers there is weakness in spreading the divine fragrances.

order.why: Place the acquisition of knowledge within prayer and effort.
shortened: My Lord, assist Thy loved ones to acquire diverse sciences and arts, to discover the mysteries treasured within the reality of created things, to become aware of the integrated symbols embedded in the essence of beings.
This greatest guidance is conditional upon and dependent on knowledge, wisdom and awareness of the mysteries of divine words.

Therefore, the friends of God, young and old, men and women, must strive to the extent possible to acquire sciences and knowledge, increase their understanding of the mysteries of the Holy Books, and gain proficiency in presenting divine proofs and evidences.

order.why: Ask how learning can become a veil.
shortened: We have decreed, O people, that the highest and last end of all learning be the recognition of Him Who is the Object of all knowledge; and yet, behold how ye have allowed your learning to shut you out, as by a veil, from Him Who is the Dayspring of this Light, through Whom every hidden thing hath been revealed.

order.why: Consider the purpose of learning in the supplied fragment.
End with intelligence bringing goodness and truth into the world.

questions: How can an argument help us move beyond inherited opinion without making us overconfident in our own reasoning?
What is the difference between observing something directly and inferring its existence from signs?
How does Aristotle’s attention to premises change the way we assess a persuasive conclusion?
How should we examine an argument when one of its illustrations reflects an earlier scientific understanding?
What relationship do these readings suggest among rational inquiry, spiritual recognition, and the use of intelligence to promote peace?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the combination of admiration for Aristotle’s discoveries and acknowledgment of their limits.
Apply careful distinctions to the different meanings of pre-existence and origination.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Posterior Analytics I.2 · What demonstration requires
references.note: Aristotle distinguishes a demonstration that yields knowledge from an argument that merely has a syllogistic form, asking about the truth, priority, and explanatory role of its premises. Compare these requirements with the compilation’s call for clear evidence and its acknowledgment of limits.

subjects.introduction: A Greek teacher honoured by Romans and Persians alike is, for ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, a sign of how knowledge ennobles a person beyond the land of their birth. Aristotle, Plato and Socrates are praised for searching both nature and the unseen, yet Aristotle is said to have gathered only a drop from the ocean, and the most brilliant intellects never moved hearts to sacrifice as the Spirit of God moved simple souls. Bahá’u’lláh describes the sages drinking from the waters of the Prophets and singles out Socrates, who turned people from idols and was put to death for it. Plato’s own account shows that same Socrates testing those reputed to be wise and finding that honest awareness of ignorance outweighs false certainty [1]. Another counsel asks for proportion: no single statement about these figures should be mistaken for the whole picture. To walk with these philosophers is to be led toward the meeting of divine and natural philosophy, and toward the history of past ages, read for what it teaches a seeker about the reach and the limits of the mind.
subjects.arc: Begin with the universal reach of knowledge, explore education and influence, compare historical accounts, and end with the collection’s own guidance on reading them.

order.why: Explore praise for inquiry into both natural and spiritual phenomena.
shortened: The philosophers of Greece -- such as Aristotle, Socrates, Plato and others -- were devoted to the investigation of both natural and spiritual phenomena. In their schools of teaching they discoursed upon the world of nature as well as the supernatural world. Today the philosophy and logic of Aristotle are known throughout the world. Because they were interested in both natural and divine philosophy, furthering the development of the physical world of mankind as well as the intellectual, they rendered praiseworthy service to humanity.

order.why: Open with knowledge honored across national boundaries.
Read the concise account of Greek schools’ scope.
Discusses differences among Greek, Roman and Persian philosophers as a limitation of unaided reason.
Introduce Aristotle’s wide learning.
shortened: According to oriental history there have come in the past two Teachers in philosophy. The first one is Aristotle who was well-versed in all the sciences and accomplishments of his time.

order.why: Hold the value of his discoveries beside their limits.
Consider the designation of teacher in a later philosophical tradition.
Read Plato as an example of determination and influence.
Explore the reported story of education changing a pupil’s capacity.
Consider the reported use of music in preparing an audience.
Distinguish extensive learning from the transforming influence attributed to the divine spirit.
shortened: The influence of the wisest philosophers, without this Spirit Divine, has been comparatively unimportant, however extensive their learning and deep their scholarship. The unusual intellects, for instance, of Plato, Aristotle, Pliny and Socrates, have not influenced men so greatly that they have been anxious to sacrifice their lives for their teachings; whilst some of those simple men so moved humanity that thousands of men have become willing martyrs to uphold their words; for these words were inspired by the Divine Spirit of God!

order.why: Read the reported contrast between material and spiritual civilization.
Keep the stronger cultural comparison in its reported setting.
Examine the story of Lycurgus and the durability of social arrangements.
shortened: Among the Greek kings there was one named Lycurgus who was both king and philosopher. His intentions were very good. He thought to make his people equal in livelihood. He divided his kingdom's inhabitants into three parts: one part he made leaders, another part he made of original inhabitants as farmers who would cultivate and pay a tithe, and the third part he made merchants and craftsmen, mostly from foreigners, who would pay something annually.

When the people had sworn and committed to not changing these rules, he left the country, gave up his kingdom and never returned so that law would remain. The people had all sworn and did not change it for a while, but after some time it changed again and those laws were overturned.

order.why: Introduce the celebrated image of Alexander as conqueror.
shortened: There are many militarists of the ancient, conservative school who hold the opinion that Alexander of Macedon was the greatest born leader, an empire-builder, a wonderful general and a great warrior. His conquests of the East are celebrated in songs and his matchless prowess [is] the theme of many a dramatic recital.

order.why: Set that image beside the judgment of conquest’s losses.
shortened: O thou who art firm in the signs of God! Alexander of Greece sought kingship and sovereignty and world conquest in this mortal realm, and in the end it became manifest loss and great harm and severe regret.

order.why: Turn to the account linking Greek sages and prophetic wisdom. Read the longer account of sages and prophetic wisdom.
shortened: The sages aforetime acquired their knowledge from the Prophets, inasmuch as the latter were the Exponents of divine philosophy and the Revealers of heavenly mysteries. Men quaffed the crystal, living waters of Their utterance, while others satisfied themselves with the dregs.

Empedocles, who distinguished himself in philosophy, was a contemporary of David, while Pythagoras lived in the days of Solomon, son of David, and acquired Wisdom from the treasury of prophethood. It is he who claimed to have heard the whispering sound of the heavens and to have attained the station of the angels.

order.why: Read the broader claim about learning from Israel.
Notice the express appeal to eastern history.
Read the parallel statement in a synagogue address.
shortened: Even the celebrated philosophers of Greece journeyed to Jerusalem in order to study with the Israelitish sages, and many were the lessons of philosophy and wisdom they received.

order.why: Consider the account of Socrates and its stated historical source. Keep the separately supplied historical explanation intact.
Read its place within a discussion of Moses. Consider the further supplied account of Socrates and branches of learning.
shortened: Such was their progress that the philosophers of Greece would come to seek knowledge from the learned men of Israel. Among them was Socrates, who came to Syria and acquired from the children of Israel the teachings of the oneness of God and the immortality of the spirit. He then returned to Greece and promulgated these teachings, whereupon the people of that land rose up in opposition to him, accused him of impiety, arraigned him before the court, and condemned him to death by poison.

The materialistic thinkers, the Greek philosophers, and the great men of Rome who became renowned in the world were each versed in but one branch of learning. Thus Galen and Hippocrates were celebrated for their skill in medicine, Aristotle in logic and speculative reasoning, and Plato in ethics and divine philosophy.

order.why: Include the later reported question about Socrates’ journey.
Explore the supplied account of divine reality and material things.
Retain the reported remarks concerning Aristotle’s intellects and images.
Read the Báb’s criticism of particular philosophical formulations.
Explore the genealogy of philosophy through Idris and Hermes.
shortened: The philosophers have been and are of different schools. Some derived their statements from the Books of the Prophets. The first to study philosophy was Idris, hence he was named thus, and he was also called Hermes. In every tongue he has a name, and in every branch of wisdom he gave sufficient and complete explanations. After him, Balinus extracted certain sciences from the Hermetic tablets, and most philosophers derived their scientific and philosophical arts from his words and explanations.

order.why: Examine the historical example used to show disagreement in reasoning.
shortened: They would even change their own views: for twenty years they would deduce the existence of something through rational arguments, and then afterwards they would disprove the same, again through rational arguments. Even Plato at first proved through rational arguments the immobility of the earth and the movement of the sun, and then subsequently established, again through rational arguments, the centrality of the sun and the movement of the earth. Then the Ptolemaic theory became widespread and Plato's theory was entirely forgotten until a modern astronomer revived it.

order.why: Preserve the fragment and its substantial supplied notes on attribution.
Read the counsel to round out a picture with other statements.
shortened: We must not take many of `Abdu'l-Baha's statements as dogmatic finalities, for there are other points which when added to them round out the picture.

Historians cannot be sure Socrates did not visit the Holy Land. But believing as we do that 'Abdu'l-Baha had an intuitive knowledge quite different from our own, we accept His authority on the matter...

order.why: Acknowledge the explicit statement about the absence of historical proof.
End with the distinction between spiritual illustration and historical endorsement.

questions: What enables knowledge to become a gift across the boundaries of language, culture, or nation?
How do the readings both honor philosophical achievement and point to its limits?
What does Plato’s portrayal of Socrates add to the collection’s accounts of wisdom, spiritual purpose, and opposition?
How should the final distinction between illustration and historical endorsement affect our reading of stories about ancient philosophers?
What might a fruitful relationship between scholarship, character, and spiritual inquiry look like in education today?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the account of reasoning from known premises toward previously unknown truths.
Consider the cultivation of outward attainments together with spiritual perfections.

references.label: 1 · Plato, Apology 20e–23b · Socrates examines wisdom
references.note: Plato’s Socrates relates the Delphic oracle and his examination of people reputed to be wise, finding a difference between knowledge and unwarranted certainty. This primary Greek portrayal offers a comparison with the collection’s later accounts; it does not independently verify their claims about travel or chronology.

subjects.displayTitle: Matter’s journeys: continuity through changing forms
subjects.introduction: The flower on the table is older than it looks. Each element in it, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observes, once lay in the mineral kingdom and wore a thousand forms there before it rose into the plant; one day it was in the sea, another in the air, another a raindrop, a bird, a human body. Nothing on this journey is destroyed; the particle is only transferred, and in every kingdom it reflects a different perfection, so that the saying that all things are involved in all things becomes a sober description. Yet the powers of a living whole are not the properties of its parts. Lucretius followed rain into grain and fruit to argue that nature reduces nothing to nothing, an ancient kinship that stops short of the theological meaning ‘Abdu’l-Bahá draws [1]. Circulation becomes a way of seeing divine bounty flow through every rank of being, and it leads on to the degrees of spirit in the kingdoms of existence, to the claim that elementary matter cannot be annihilated, and to the long question of evolution.
subjects.arc: Begin with the flower, follow circulation through living forms, distinguish constituent identity from emergent powers, and explore the spiritual analogies drawn from change.

order.why: Follow the vivid sequence of sea, land, cloud, and living forms.
shortened: Thus, every single elemental particle of existence transfers through infinite forms -- one day it is in the sea, another day on land, another day in the air, another day it is rain, another day a cloud, another day a flower, another day a human, another day an animal. That is, it journeys through all beings and in each being it possesses a distinct perfection -- in the human world it has human perfection, in the animal world animal perfection, and in the vegetable world vegetable perfection.

order.why: Open with the elements gathered into a flower.
Read the concise movement through mineral, plant, animal, and human life.
Describes material incorporation and renewal from mineral to plant, animal and human life.
Introduce the analogy of elements as letters and organisms as words.
Consider composition and the appearance of additional powers.
shortened: All things in creation are composed of simple atoms of compound particles. In the mineral kingdom, many substances such as gold are composed of simple atoms. In the vegetable kingdom, plants are composed of more complex particles, hence we see they have more qualities and powers, such as growth, for example. Then again, in the animal kingdom, the creatures are still more complex and have additional powers such as instinct, and in the kingdom of man many more powers and qualities are possessed and developed.

order.why: Distinguish the identity of a constituent from the powers of the whole.
Explore persistence through successive incorporations.
shortened: For example, an atom of the soil or dust of earth may traverse the kingdoms from mineral to man by successive incorporations into the bodies of the organisms of those kingdoms. At one time it enters into the formation of the mineral or rock; it is then absorbed by the vegetable kingdom and becomes a constituent of the body and fibre of a tree; again it is appropriated by the animal, and at a still later period is found in the body of man. Throughout these degrees of its traversing the kingdoms from one form of phenomenal being to another, it retains its atomic existence and is never annihilated nor relegated to nonexistence.

order.why: Read the fuller account of transfer and indestructibility.
shortened: In short, the single element is subjected to coursings and journeyings throughout the interminable universe, and in every stage it has certain distinct virtues. For these virtues there is no end. Thus it is evident that the single element is absolutely indestructible and eternal. It appears in all phenomena, at most being subject simply to transferences, but not to destruction. It is everlasting.

order.why: Follow the elements into the human body.
Read the parallel progression through constituent substances.
Make the account concrete through an ordinary meal.
Consider its use in a question concerning animals.
Read the language of felicity within assimilation. Read the separate supplied wording concerning felicity.
shortened: But true felicity for the animal consists in passing from the animal world into the human realm, like the microscopic beings that, through the air and the water, enter into the body of man, are assimilated, and replace that which has been consumed in his body. This is the greatest honour and felicity for the animal world, and no greater honour can be conceived for it.

order.why: Explore the image of loss opening into another form of life.
Turn toward the acquisition of powers in human existence.
shortened: We come from the earth; why were we transferred from the mineral to the vegetable kingdom -- from the plant to the animal kingdom? So that we may attain perfection in each of these kingdoms, that we may possess the best qualities of the mineral, that we may acquire the power of growing as in the plant, that we may be adorned with the instincts of the animal and possess the faculties of sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste, until from the animal kingdom we step into the world of humanity and are gifted with reason, the power of invention, and the forces of the spirit.'

order.why: Consider how material transitions become an analogy for spiritual life.
Read the differing degrees assigned to life.
shortened: In the physical creation, evolution is from one degree of perfection to another.

This world is full of seeming contradictions; in each of these kingdoms (mineral, vegetable and animal) life exists in its degree; though when compared to the life in a man, the earth appears to be dead, yet she, too, lives and has a life of her own.

order.why: Explore the idea of latent capacities appearing across environments.
shortened: From this it becomes evident that throughout countless ages, every primordial atom must journey and traverse through the infinite degrees and stations of the Kingdoms of life on this grand Cosmos. In every stage of growth and development this atom assumes unto itself a definite form and shape conformable to its environment and adaptable to its existence and possible variation until at last it attains to its highest point of progress, displaying all its latent force of variability and development.

order.why: Consider the abstract claim that a particle can reflect the virtues of many forms. Read the statement concerning perpetual motion.
shortened: The elemental atoms which constitute all phenomenal existence and being in this illimitable universe are in perpetual motion, undergoing continuous degrees of progression.

In its ceaseless progression and journeyings the atom becomes imbued with the virtues and powers of each degree or kingdom it traverses. In the degree of the mineral it possessed mineral affinities; in the kingdom of the vegetable it manifested the augmentative virtue or power of growth; in the animal organism it reflected the intelligence of that degree; and in the kingdom of man it was qualified with human attributes or virtues.
It is evident, then, that each elemental atom of the universe is possessed of a capacity to express all the virtues of the universe.

order.why: Close the linked readings with another historical account of atomism.
shortened: Al-Ash'ari says about it: [']The entire creation consists of matter and power (movement). Matter, the corporeal, consists of atoms which are alike; they, the atoms, fill up space, they are units without magnitude conceived as points, on which all spatial corporeal existence is based. The atoms do not penetrate into each other, they move, they change. All changes of the atoms are based on combination and separation, on quick and undetectable movement -on this is dependent the form, the appearance of the body.

order.why: Revisit the supplied account of journeys through kingdoms.
Consider organisms as aggregates expressing other phenomena.
shortened: It is evident that each material organism is an aggregate expression of single and simple elements, and a given cellular element or atom has its coursings or journeyings through various and myriad stages of life. For example, we will say the cellular elements which have entered into the composition of a human organism were at one time a component part of the animal kingdom; at another time they entered into the composition of the vegetable, and prior to that they existed in the kingdom of the mineral.

order.why: Keep the historical formulation concerning conservation in its original terms.
Explore capacities manifested in a different realm.
shortened: For it is clear, evident, and indeed obvious that every capacity, merit, power and perfection that any thing acquires in one rank of existence becomes manifest when it is raised to the rank above it.

For instance, the capacities and bestowals that the mineral acquires in the mineral world do not become visible in the mineral world, but rather when it transfers from the mineral world to the vegetable world, that inherent gift is unveiled. And when the plant acquires the capacity to develop a sensitive body in the vegetable world, this perfection appears upon its transfer to the animal world.

order.why: End with material circulation as an image of circulating divine bestowals.
Consider the further image of myriad transferences.
Widen the image to an infinity of forms.

questions: How does imagining the prior and future journeys of the elements in a flower change the way we see it?
What distinction do these passages make between a material constituent and the powers of the living whole to which it belongs?
How does Lucretius’s account of rain and nourishment resemble these descriptions, and how do their larger philosophical purposes differ?
What can a material transformation illuminate about spiritual development, and where might the analogy reach its limits?
How could reflection on interdependence influence the way we care for living things and the material conditions they share?

neighbors.invitation: Distinguish continuity in creation from independence of a cause.
Explore the different claim that the human spirit acquires perfections through the degrees of existence.

references.label: 1 · Lucretius, On the Nature of Things I · Rain, nourishment, and renewal
references.note: In Book I, the passage describing rain, grain, fruit, and nourishment illustrates the claim that things are rebuilt from other things rather than reduced to nothing. Compare this account of material continuity with the compilation’s journeys through forms, while distinguishing ancient atomism from both modern physics and the theological meanings given here.

subjects.introduction: To ask when the world began is one question; to ask what holds it in being is another, and Bahá’u’lláh answers the second with an image of a sprinkling from the deep of God’s Will calling into existence, out of utter nothingness, a creation without end. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá presses the logic: there can be no Creator without a creation, so to give creation a beginning would be to give God one. Yet nothingness remains part of the vocabulary, in prayers that praise the One who brought the subtlest elements out of naught and in the plain statement that the globe is millions of years old while its Creator has no age at all. The reconciliation lies in a distinction between temporal and essential origination: a thing may have no first moment and still depend wholly on its cause. Aquinas reasoned nearby when he held that the world’s temporal beginning is an article of faith rather than something philosophy can prove, and separated being made from beginning in time [1]; his different conclusion makes the comparison instructive. The same language of creation returns whenever a Manifestation appears and souls are made new. From here the inquiry turns to the continual renewal of creation, the ceaseless divine emanation, the creation of the world, and the covenant taken on the day of Alast.
subjects.arc: Begin with the apparent paradox of creation without beginning, introduce distinctions of cause and time, then read symbolic nothingness alongside renewal and gratitude.

order.why: Open with beginningless creation described as called from nothingness.
shortened: A sprinkling from the unfathomed deep of His sovereign and all-pervasive Will hath, out of utter nothingness, called into being a creation which is infinite in its range and deathless in its duration.  The wonders of His bounty can never cease, and the stream of His merciful grace can never be arrested.  The process of His creation hath had no beginning, and can have no end.

order.why: Explore the argument from divine names and attributes.
Read the explicit account of an unending creative power.
Consider the concise relation of creator and creation.
Read the further statement of divine pre-existence and creation.
Explains creation ex nihilo through divine will while rejecting connection or likeness between the divine Essence and creation.
Distinguish the age of the world from a short literal chronology.
Hear the reported contrast between an ancient globe and its creator.
Consider the phrase beginning that has no beginning.
shortened: He has ever been in the heights of exaltation, grandeur and glory, and will ever be in the summit of might, power and majesty, even as He was in the beginning that has no beginning.

order.why: Set this beside a prayer of divine existence before and after all things.
Read the language of the creative command and emergence into being.
shortened: No sign can indicate His presence or His absence; inasmuch as by a word of His command all that are in heaven and on earth have come to exist, and by His wish, which is the Primal Will itself, all have stepped out of utter nothingness into the realm of being, the world of the visible.

order.why: Keep the parallel formulation distinct.
Connect emergence with the means of elevation.
Explore the use of creation language at the appearance of a Manifestation.
Close the linked readings with a personal address about existence and education.
Introduce the explicit distinction between essential and temporal origination.
shortened: Answer: Certain sages and philosophers hold that there are two kinds of pre-existence, essential and temporal, and that there are likewise two kinds of origination, essential and temporal.

Essential pre-existence is an existence which is not preceded by a cause; essential origination is preceded by a cause. Temporal pre-existence has no beginning; temporal origination has both a beginning and an end.

order.why: Read the related account of two kinds of eternity.
Connect beginningless creation with its dependence on a cause.
Examine the argument concerning absolute nonexistence.
Consider the stated inner meaning of a short creation chronology.
Read the subtle distinction concerning a firstness unlike temporal firstness.
shortened: Indeed He was a hidden treasure. This is a station that can never be described nor even alluded to. And in the station of 'I did wish to make Myself known', God was, and His creation had ever existed beneath His shelter from the beginning that hath no beginning, apart from its being preceded by a Firstness which cannot be regarded as firstness and originated by a Cause inscrutable even unto all men of learning.

order.why: Preserve the Báb’s further metaphysical account.
shortened: When the existence of the Eternal Essence is established through His own existence and not through any other - as indicated by "O Thou Who hast proven Thy Essence by Thy Essence!" - then the existence of originated things is established through creation itself, not from anything else.

order.why: Read the symbolic interpretation preserved in the supplied citation note.
Hear the Báb’s account of the potency of the command.
Read the concise prayer of creation from naught.
Connect origination with return to God.
Revisit divine existence above and beyond things.
shortened: Thou art He Who existed before all things in the eternity of Thine essence, and Thou art He Who will endure after all things in the everlastingness of Thine existence.

order.why: Turn from beginninglessness to renewal in revelation.
Consider the invitation to seek what is enduring.
shortened: O servant of God! Days shall pass and times shall come to an end, but the favors of the Blessed Beauty shall remain steadfast and enduring, and the bounties of the Most Great Name shall eternally embrace the everlasting and the infinite. Therefore seek thou that which is eternal, and desire thou that which is everlasting.

order.why: Include Augustine’s question about time before creation.
Consider existence as a bestowed garment.
Retain the brief supplied affirmation of creation.

questions: How does distinguishing a beginning in time from dependence on a cause change the questions we ask about creation?
How can the language of nothingness function differently in a prayer, a philosophical argument, and an account of spiritual renewal?
What is clarified by comparing Aquinas’s position on a temporal beginning with the beginningless creation described in these selections?
How does the image of a new creation at the appearance of revelation connect cosmic language with human experience?
What difference might it make to understand existence as continually dependent on bounty rather than simply as something that happened long ago?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the distinction between what is unprecedented and what is impossible.
Explore the relation between persistence of constituents and changing forms.

references.label: 1 · Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, question 46, article 2 · What reason can establish
references.note: Aquinas treats the world’s temporal beginning as an article of faith rather than a demonstrable conclusion. In his replies he distinguishes being made from beginning in time. Compare that distinction and his different conclusion with the accounts of essential and temporal origination in this compilation.

subjects.displayTitle: Human potential: bringing hidden gifts into life
subjects.introduction: A gem lies in the ground long before anyone knows how to bring it out, and Bahá’u’lláh says that God reveals Himself for exactly that purpose: to lay bare the gems hidden in the mine of our inmost selves. He adds that His creation in each of us is already perfected; what remains is to let its excellence show. The images that follow are all images of labour: a tree watered with uprightness and understanding, a mirror polished by striving, a child trained to become a lighted candle, growth measured day by day. Potential, on this account, is not status or a single triumph but knowledge, character and deeds that benefit others, and this life is the womb in which the powers needed for the next are acquired. Aristotle, distinguishing a capacity from a formed virtue and locating the difference in repeated action, offers a practical companion to that patience [1], though the two accounts place the source of fulfilment differently. Progress continues without any final claim to perfection, and another person’s gifts may be larger than our present view of them. The path leads on to the development of capacity and readiness, the universal human capacity for spiritual recognition, and the fruit every life is meant to bear.
subjects.arc: Begin with hidden value, explore education and transformation, connect growth with service, and end with ongoing refinement and hope for every buried gem.

order.why: Open with the hidden gems within a person’s inmost self.
shortened: The Purpose of the one true God, exalted be His glory, in revealing Himself unto men is to lay bare those gems that lie hidden within the mine of their true and inmost selves.

order.why: Establish confidence in the endowment while naming the veil of desire.
Develop the image through nourishment of human trees.
Explore the unveiling of the divine trust. Consider the unfolding of the forces latent within a person.
shortened: Through the Teachings of this Daystar of Truth every man will advance and develop until he attaineth the station at which he can manifest all the potential forces with which his inmost true self hath been endowed. It is for this very purpose that in every age and dispensation the Prophets of God and His chosen Ones have appeared amongst men, and have evinced such power as is born of God and such might as only the Eternal can reveal.

order.why: Read the related imagery of gems and the purpose of revelation.
shortened: These words have streamed from the pen of this Wronged One in one of His Tablets: "The purpose of the one true God, exalted be His glory, hath been to bring forth the Mystic Gems out of the mine of man -- they Who are the Dawning-Places of His Cause and the Repositories of the pearls of His knowledge; for, God Himself, glorified be He, is the Unseen, the One concealed and hidden from the eyes of men.

order.why: Consider the awakening of latent human virtues.
Make transformation concrete through ignorance, injustice, and cruelty. Revisit the transformation of ignorance and cruelty in the separate excerpt.
shortened: The aim of the prophet of God is to raise man to the degree of knowledge of his potentiality and to illumine him through the light of the kingdom, to transform ignorance into wisdom, injustice into justice, error into knowledge, cruelty into affection and incapability into progress. In short, to make all the attainments of existence resplendent in him.

order.why: Bring the theme into the education of children.
Join outward attainments with spiritual perfections.
Set growth within a daily rhythm.
Connect effort in virtue with progress.
Direct effort toward becoming a source of good.
Explore the images of orchards, gardens, and lamps.
Consider the transformation of character in a person.
Read the reported examples of Peter and Mary Magdalene.
Widen the horizon through the promise of continuing progress.
shortened: Ye are the children of God and he has endowed you with the possibilities of infinite progress.

order.why: Consider the purpose of the spirit’s passage through degrees.
Read the aspiration toward human excellences.
shortened: It is the desire of my heart and soul that in this path ye may travel along all the degrees of existence and attain to the loftiest horizon of the ideal virtues and the pinnacles of human excellences; - in order that all the people may witness how the servants of His Highness the Friend are illumined, shining and radiant.

order.why: Connect fulfillment with the person’s kind or station.
Explore the seed and fruit analogy in its reported use of Nirvana.
Read the image of humanity’s promised station.
Keep the supplied description of perfection in its own context.
shortened: Human life and spiritual living consist in attaining perfection in all stations - absolutely no deficiency remained in any aspect. In all conditions he was assisted by the favors of the Incomparable Lord.

order.why: Explains each soul’s individual capacity and possibility of developing spiritual light.
Consider the fruits of labor and happiness.
shortened: A person characterized with these attributes will gather the fruits of his labors and will win the happiness of the kingdom.

order.why: Read the image of the true fruit of existence.
Hear the celebratory account of life’s outcome.
shortened: This is the outcome of life! This is the result of ceaseless endeavour! This is the prize to be won! This is the illumination of the world of humanity! This is Eternal Life! This is the sublimity of human nature! This is the Heavenly Glory! This is the radiant crown of the Kingdom of Abha!

order.why: Close the linked sequence with service, human oneness, and peace.
Return to education as the means of revealing treasures.
shortened: Men at all times and under all conditions stand in need of one to exhort them, guide them and to instruct and teach them.  Therefore He hath sent forth His Messengers, His Prophets and chosen ones that they might acquaint the people with the divine purpose underlying the revelation of Books and the raising up of Messengers, and that every- one may become aware of the trust of God which is latent in the reality of every soul.

order.why: Consider present life as preparation through acquired capacities.
shortened: Therefore, in this world he must prepare himself for the life beyond. That which he needs in the world of the Kingdom must be obtained here. Just as he prepared himself in the world of the matrix by acquiring forces necessary in this sphere of existence, so, likewise, the indispensable forces of the divine existence must be potentially attained in this world.

That world beyond is a world of sanctity and radiance; therefore, it is necessary that in this world he should acquire these divine attributes. In that world there is need of spirituality, faith, assurance, the knowledge and love of God. These he must attain in this world so that after his ascension from the earthly to the heavenly Kingdom he shall find all that is needful in that eternal life ready for him.

order.why: Read the role assigned to innate powers and response.
shortened: He Who is the Dayspring of Truth is, no doubt, fully capable of rescuing from such remoteness wayward souls and of causing them to draw nigh unto His court and attain His Presence. “If God had pleased He had surely made all men one people.” His purpose, however, is to enable the pure in spirit and the detached in heart to ascend, by virtue of their own innate powers, unto the shores of the Most Great Ocean, that thereby they who seek the Beauty of the All-Glorious may be distinguished and separated from the wayward and perverse. Thus hath it been ordained by the all-glorious and resplendent Pen.

order.why: Hold refinement beside the supplied clarification about continuing progress.
shortened: Through the pure bounty of His grace and the sublime excellence of His mercy, He hath deposited within all things that are seen and known the sign of His knowledge, that no thing might be deprived of recognizing His presence according to its capacity and station. And this sign is the mirror of His beauty in creation, and the more this most exalted, most wondrous, and most impregnable mirror is polished through striving and endeavor, the more shall the manifestations of His names and attributes and the evidences of His knowledge and signs be impressed and reflected therein, to such degree that every thing may witness in its place and every thing may know its limit and measure, and may hear from all things that there is no God but Him and that 'Ali-Qabli-Nabil is the Manifestation of all names and the Dawning-Place of all attributes, that all were created by His will and all act by His command.

order.why: Connect development of the mind with selflessness and peace.
End with the hope that even a deeply buried gem can be found.

questions: How would education change if it began with confidence in hidden value that may not yet be visible?
What do the different images of a mine, a tree, and a mirror suggest about the work of developing human capacities?
How does Aristotle’s emphasis on repeated action help make the cultivation of virtue practical?
How can we encourage ambitious effort while remembering the distinction between continuing progress and a final state of perfection?
What opportunities in ordinary community life might reveal capacities in ourselves or others that have remained unnoticed?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the purpose of intellect in creating love and bringing people together.
Explore the connection between freedom of spirit, nobility, and human happiness.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 · Becoming through practice
references.note: Aristotle distinguishes having a capacity from developing a virtue and argues that character is formed through repeated activities. Compare this account of habituation with the compilation’s education, spiritual guidance, and daily effort; their accounts of the source and purpose of human fulfillment differ.

subjects.displayTitle: True liberty: freedom with a purpose
subjects.introduction: After forty years as a prisoner, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá could say he knew the value of liberty, and also that no fortress had ever confined him. Both statements are true, and the subject lives in their tension. Physical freedom is a good thing, constitutions and the rights of all subjects deserve support, and peace itself is called the freedom of the world; yet the person driven by appetite is captive to nature, and unchecked licence is the freedom of the animal. Bahá’u’lláh therefore speaks of a liberty found in submission to divine law, a claim that asks careful thought about what freedom is for. Epictetus, locating freedom in the right use of what lies within our control, offers a Stoic comparison to a spirit that soars while the body lies in a dungeon [1]. True liberty is finally bound to fellowship, moral education and the release of the downtrodden from their chains. From here the road leads into freedom of thought and action, the independent investigation of truth, and the relationship between a government and its people.
subjects.arc: Begin with the felt value of release, distinguish inward and outward freedom, examine liberty and restraint, and end with service and responsibility to others.

order.why: Read the complex counsel on legitimate liberty and moderation.
shortened: True Democrats are souls who seek the freedom of humanity, who hold to legitimate liberty, who establish constitutional government, and who desire good for all on earth. I hope they will take the path of moderation, abandon savagery, seek tranquility and pursue legitimate freedom. Do not quarrel and dispute with such persons now present in Iran. If possible, invite them to reality, saying: "O seeker of freedom! This supposed freedom of yours is bondage to chains and fetters. It is constraint, not freedom; it is shackles, not aspiration and nobility; it is the darkness of prison, not the light of the palace."

order.why: Read the reported appreciation of public liberty.
Open with the testimony of someone who knows imprisonment.
Distinguishes release from prison from the true freedom of immersion in divine love.
Set outward confinement beside an unconquered spirit.
Distinguish physical and spiritual freedom while valuing both.
Consider freedom of rights and constitutional government.
Value freedom independently of whether repression aids a religious cause.
shortened: He [Abdu'l-Baha] replied that, "In principle, we prefer freedom as it is one of the divine blessings and pleases God. However, this is not because freedom helps with the diffusion and propagation of our Cause, as it is the opposite -- namely, our Cause grows better in a repressive environment."

order.why: Connect universal peace with freedom.
Follow peace into joy and useful work.
Explore fellowship and love as conditions of true liberty. Apply the principle of moderation to authority and civilization.
shortened: If the learned and worldly-wise men of this age were to allow mankind to inhale the fragrance of fellowship and love, every understanding heart would apprehend the meaning of true liberty, and discover the secret of undisturbed peace and absolute composure.

It is incumbent upon them who are in authority to exercise moderation in all things.  Whatsoever passeth beyond the limits of moderation will cease to exert a beneficial influence.  Consider for instance such things as liberty, civilization and the like.  However much men of understanding may favourably regard them, they will, if carried to excess, exercise a pernicious influence upon men.

order.why: Connect release from discord with freedom.
Ask what it means to be free from captivity to nature.
Distinguish absence of restraint from human freedom. Read the fuller distinction among divine, political, and spiritual freedom. Keep the separate supplied version and its provenance intact.
shortened: There are three types of freedom.
There is a divine freedom, and this is peculiar unto the Essence of the Creator; for He is absolutely free.

The second is the political freedom of Europeans, which leaves the individual free to do whatsoever he desires as long as his action does not harm his neighbour. This is natural freedom, and its greatest expression is seen in the animal world. Observe these birds and notice with what freedom they live. However much man may try, he can never be as free as an animal, because the existence of order acts as an impediment to freedom.
The third freedom is that which is born of obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Almighty. This is the freedom of the human world, where man severs his affections from all things.

order.why: Read the reported concern about education and sudden political change.
Consider liberation from oppression and treachery through the divine word.
shortened: And necessarily for every matter there is a center - the center of this overwhelming power is the Manifestation of God's commanding Word and His prevailing Cause, who without imprisonment and politics liberates souls from the bonds of oppression and treachery.

order.why: Explore the image of a charter of liberty.
shortened: He Who had been concealed from men's eyes is now come. How good is His coming! In one hand He is carrying the water of life and in the other the charter of true liberty.

order.why: Give the summons a universal scope. End with action for the peace and well-being of the downtrodden.
shortened: Arise for the triumph of My Cause, and, through the power of thine utterance, subdue the hearts of men. Thou must show forth that which will ensure the peace and the well-being of the miserable and the downtrodden. Gird up the loins of thine endeavour, that perchance thou mayest release the captive from his chains, and enable him to attain unto true liberty.

The summons and the message which We gave were never intended to reach or to benefit one land or one people only. Mankind in its entirety must firmly adhere to whatsoever hath been revealed and vouchsafed unto it. Then and only then will it attain unto true liberty.

order.why: Return to freedom beyond chains and worldly attachment.
Read the parallel assurance of freedom in the kingdom.
Consider the paradox of captivity to the Holy Spirit.
Close the linked readings with happiness and freedom of spirit.
Revisit the relation of restraint to protection. Read the positive definition of liberty through servitude to God.
shortened: That which beseemeth man is submission unto such restraints as will protect him from his own ignorance, and guard him against the harm of the mischief-maker.

Say: True liberty consisteth in man's submission unto My commandments, little as ye know it. Were men to observe that which We have sent down unto them from the Heaven of Revelation, they would, of a certainty, attain unto perfect liberty. Happy is the man that hath apprehended the Purpose of God in whatever He hath revealed from the Heaven of His Will that pervadeth all created things. Say: The liberty that profiteth you is to be found nowhere except in complete servitude unto God, the Eternal Truth. Whoso hath tasted of its sweetness will refuse to barter it for all the dominion of earth and heaven.

order.why: Read the relation between accepted imprisonment and others’ liberation.
shortened: The Ancient Beauty hath consented to be bound with chains that mankind may be released from its bondage, and hath accepted to be made a prisoner within this most mighty Stronghold that the whole world may attain unto true liberty. He hath drained to its dregs the cup of sorrow, that all the peoples of the earth may attain unto abiding joy, and be filled with gladness. This is of the mercy of your Lord, the Compassionate, the Most Merciful. We have accepted to be abased, O believers in the Unity of God, that ye may be exalted, and have suffered manifold afflictions, that ye might prosper and flourish.

order.why: Consider the later exposition of these statements.
shortened: Expounding the theme of liberty, Baha'u'llah asserted that "the embodiment of liberty and its symbol is the animal"; that "liberty causeth man to overstep the bounds of propriety, and to infringe on the dignity of his station"; that "true liberty consisteth in man's submission unto My commandments". "We approve of liberty in certain circumstances," He declared, "and refuse to sanction it in others." But He gave the assurance that, "Were men to observe that which We have sent down unto them from the Heaven of Revelation, they would, of a certainty, attain unto perfect liberty."

order.why: Read the warning against both extreme orthodoxy and irresponsible freedom.
Include the literary criticism of endlessly multiplying needs.

questions: How do the readings distinguish outward liberty from inward freedom, and why does each matter?
When might satisfying a desire enlarge a person’s freedom, and when might it deepen dependence?
How does Epictetus’s distinction between what we control and what we do not illuminate the accounts of freedom in prison?
What makes the claim that obedience can liberate intelligible, and what questions about conscience and responsibility does it raise?
How can the counsels on fellowship, rights, and care for the downtrodden prevent inward freedom from becoming indifference to other people’s circumstances?

neighbors.invitation: Explore freedom through deeds beneficial to humanity and service to peace.
Bring reasoned examination to inherited ideas about liberty and responsibility.

references.label: 1 · Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 · What is within our control
references.note: Epictetus distinguishes judgment and choice from external possessions, reputation, and bodily circumstances, connecting freedom with the former. Compare this Stoic discipline with the compilation’s spiritual freedom, while also attending to its affirmative concern for rights and liberation from oppression.
